Communicative grammar means understanding how grammar creates meaning in real communication: subject-verb agreement, verb tenses, fragments, run-ons, modifiers and articles. In this unit's account, "register" refers to: (Remember) a) a list of vocabulary words b) the level of formality a situation demands c) the pronunciation of a word d) the spelling of a word A teacher says, "The pupils in Class 7 reads quietly." The three topics follow the logic of a single lesson. Topic 1.1 asks what words mean in context and how grammar creates meaning. Topic 1.2 asks how words are built and how sentences are structured. Topic 1.3 asks how the sounds of English carry meaning. Each topic builds on the previous one, so teach them in order across the four weeks the content-spec allows.

"Vocabulary means memorising long word lists." This is the most persistent one. Probe it by asking: "If you know the meaning of 'run' but not its collocations, can you use it correctly?" Trainees who equate vocabulary with word lists will find the register and collocation sections counter-intuitive. "Grammar rules are fixed and universal." Probe it by asking: "If grammar is fixed, why do British and American English differ in their use of the present perfect?" The goal is to shift from rule-memorisation to understanding how grammar creates meaning. "Pronunciation does not matter as long as people understand you." Probe it by asking: "If someone says 'I need a pin' and you hear 'I need a fin', has communication succeeded?" The goal is to make the case that clarity matters, not accent.

Topic 1.1 - Analyse a text for vocabulary and grammar (25 minutes, pairs). The trap is that trainees identify words without explaining their context-dependence. Push them back: "What does this word mean in THIS context, and how do you know?" Circulate and listen for explanations that go beyond dictionary definitions. Topic 1.2 - Analyse word formation and sentence structure (25 minutes, groups of three). The trap is that trainees classify sentences by length rather than by clause structure. Remind them: "A long sentence can be simple; a short sentence can be complex. Count the clauses, not the words." Topic 1.3 - Minimal pairs practice (15 minutes, pairs). This is a quick, active exercise. The key teaching move is the debrief: ask which pairs were hardest and why. The answer will almost always be the pairs involving sounds that do not exist in Urdu.

Each topic carries a "Try this at your practicum school" task. The unit works best when the tutor sets these up explicitly before trainees leave for practicum and debriefs them when trainees return. Topic 1.1 practicum task (collect pupil writing samples) produces a small data set. Use it to open Topic 1.2: ask trainees which vocabulary issues were most common, and use their examples to motivate the word-formation section. Topic 1.2 practicum task (analyse textbook material) produces a comparison. Use it to make the point that textbooks vary in the sentence structures they present, and that pupils need exposure to all four. Topic 1.3 practicum task (record a teacher reading) produces a pronunciation analysis. Use it to make the point that even fluent teachers have pronunciation features that may confuse pupils.

The unit carries six figures: two concept-map figures (fig-U1-1, fig-U1-5), two diagram figures (fig-U1-2, fig-U1-3), and two table figures (fig-U1-4, fig-U1-6). The tables are the ones trainees most often try to read as prose. Before you project any of them, ask trainees to read the column headers first and say what the table is comparing.

The 10/10/5 bank is designed to be used in two passes: the MCQs and RRQs as formative checks at the end of Topics 1.2 and 1.3, and the ERQs as a summative task at the end of the unit. ERQ 5 (the integrative item) is the one that most reliably separates trainees who have understood the unit from those who have memorised its definitions. If you use only one ERQ, use that one.

Unit 1 gave you the building blocks of English: words, grammar, sounds. This unit asks what happens when you put those blocks together to read and listen. A text is not just a collection of sentences; it is a communication shaped by who wrote it, for whom, and for what purpose. This unit gives you the skills to read between the lines.

By the end of this unit you should be able to: Explain how purpose, audience and context shape a text and influence the choices a writer makes. Identify tone, bias, stereotypes, assumptions and inferences in a text. Apply reading strategies (skimming, scanning, SQ4R, critical reading) to different kinds of text. Practise active listening and apply strategies for overcoming listening barriers. Analyse a described text for what it says, what it implies, and what it assumes.
Unit 1, in particular the vocabulary and grammar foundations. This unit assumes you can identify sentence structures and word classes and applies those skills to the analysis of whole texts.

Topic 2.1 - Reading for purpose, audience and context - how purpose, audience and context shape a text; identifying tone, bias and assumptions. Topic 2.2 - Strategies for reading and listening - skimming, scanning, SQ4R, critical reading; active listening and note-taking. Topic 2.3 - Critical reading and listening in practice - applying comprehension and analysis skills to a described text.

The three topics follow the logic of a single reading event. Topic 2.1 asks what the writer brought to the text; Topic 2.2 asks what strategies you bring as a reader; Topic 2.3 asks you to combine both in practice. Work through them in order.

textbook.com.pk Mr Sajid teaches Class 10 English in a government school in Lahore. He gives his pupils two texts about the same topic: a newspaper editorial and a textbook chapter. The editorial argues that mobile phones should be banned in schools; the textbook chapter explains how mobile networks work. Same topic, completely different texts. This topic is about why.
A text does not exist in a vacuum. It is written by someone, for someone, for a reason. Understanding these three elements, purpose, audience and context, is the first step in reading critically.

Purpose is why a text was written. A text may aim to inform (a textbook), persuade (an editorial), entertain (a novel), instruct (a manual) or express (a poem). Most texts have more than one purpose, but one is usually dominant. Identifying the dominant purpose helps you understand what the writer is trying to achieve. Audience is who the text is written for. A text for specialists uses technical language; a text for general readers does not. A text for children uses simpler sentence structures than a text for adults. Identifying the intended audience helps you understand the choices the writer has made. Context is the situation in which the text was produced and is being read. A news article written during an election has a different context from one written during peacetime. A textbook written for Pakistani schools has a different context from one written for British schools. Context shapes what can be said and how it can be said. The figure above maps the elements of purpose, audience and context and the features they produce.

Tone is the writer's attitude toward the subject or the audience. A text can be formal or informal, serious or humorous, respectful or sarcastic. Tone is created through word choice, sentence structure and the details the writer includes or leaves out. Bias is a tendency to favour one perspective over others. All texts have some bias; the question is whether the bias is acknowledged or hidden. A biased text presents one side of an argument as if it were the only side. Stereotype is a fixed, oversimplified belief about a group of people. Texts can reinforce stereotypes (women are emotional, rural people are ignorant) or challenge them. Identifying stereotypes is part of reading critically. Assumption is something the writer takes for granted without stating it explicitly. A text that says "obviously, all parents want their children to succeed" assumes that this is universal. Identifying assumptions is part of understanding what a text does not say. Inference is a conclusion the reader draws from evidence in the text. If a text says "the pupils entered the examination hall in silence and sat without speaking", you can infer that they were nervous, even though the text does not say so directly. textbook.com.pk The figure above maps common biases and stereotypes with examples from Pakistani media. Use it as a reference when you analyse texts. Common misconception. "A text means what it says and nothing more." It does not. Every text contains assumptions, inferences and biases that the reader must identify. Reading critically means reading what is there and what is not there.

Work in pairs. Take two texts on the same topic (a newspaper editorial and a textbook chapter, or a government pamphlet and a blog post). For each text, identify: the dominant purpose, the intended audience, the context, the tone, and at least one assumption or bias. Allow 25 minutes. Then compare with another pair and discuss any disagreements.

(Analyze) Explain the difference between what a text says explicitly and what the reader infers, and give one example of each. (Understand)

Purpose, audience and context shape every text. Tone, bias, stereotypes, assumptions and inferences are the features a critical reader identifies. Reading critically means reading what is there and what is not there, and understanding the choices the writer has made.

textbook.com.pk Miss Fatima teaches Class 8 English in a government school in Peshawar. She gives her pupils a three-page textbook chapter and tells them to read it. Some pupils read every word from start to finish and remember little. Others look at the headings first and do better. This topic is about why some reading strategies work better than others.
Good readers do not read every text the same way. They adjust their strategy to their purpose. This topic covers the main reading strategies and the listening strategies that complement them.

textbook.com.pk The figure above maps the main reading strategies and when to use each one. Skimming is reading quickly to get the main idea of a text. You read the title, the headings, the first and last paragraphs, and any bold or italic text. Skimming answers the question: "What is this text about, and do I need to read it in more detail?" It is the right strategy when you are deciding whether a text is relevant. Scanning is reading quickly to find specific information. You look for a name, a date, a number or a keyword. Scanning answers the question: "Does this text contain the information I need?" It is the right strategy when you know what you are looking for. SQ4R is a structured strategy for reading a text in depth. The figure above maps the steps: Survey (skim the text to get an overview), Question (turn each heading into a question), Read (read to answer the question), Recite (summarise the answer in your own words), Review (go back and check your understanding), Reflect (connect the content to what you already know). SQ4R is the right strategy when you need to understand and remember a text. Critical reading is reading to evaluate a text, not just understand it. You ask: What is the writer's purpose? What assumptions are being made? What evidence is provided? What is left out? Critical reading is the right strategy when you need to assess the quality or reliability of a text.

Active listening is listening with the intention to understand, not just to hear. It is the aural equivalent of critical reading. The guide lists several barriers to active listening and strategies for overcoming them. Overcoming listening barriers. Common barriers include distractions (noise, movement, daydreaming), bias (stopping listening when you disagree), and language difficulty (losing the thread when the speaker uses unfamiliar vocabulary). Strategies include: sitting where you can hear clearly, focusing on the speaker rather than your own thoughts, and noting key words rather than trying to understand every word. Focused listening is listening for a specific purpose. If you are listening for the main idea, you focus on the introduction and conclusion. If you are listening for detail, you focus on specific facts and figures. If you are listening for tone, you focus on the speaker's voice and word choice. Note-taking is recording what you hear in a way that helps you remember and review. The figure above maps common note-taking formats: linear notes (headings and bullet points), mind maps (branches radiating from a central idea), and Cornell notes (a divided page with cues, notes and a summary). Different formats suit different purposes. Common misconception. "Listening is a passive skill." It is not. Active listening requires focus, strategy and engagement, just like critical reading.

Work alone. Take a three-page English text (a textbook chapter, a newspaper feature, or an academic article). Apply the six steps of SQ4R: survey, question, read, recite, review, reflect. Allow 30 minutes. Then compare your notes with a partner and discuss which steps were most useful.

(Understand) A friend says, "I just listen and hope I will remember." Using this topic's account, explain why this approach is unreliable and propose three specific strategies. (Apply) Describe the Cornell note-taking format and explain when it is most useful. (Remember)

Reading strategies (skimming, scanning, SQ4R, critical reading) are tools that good readers choose according to their purpose. Active listening requires focus, strategy and engagement. Note-taking formats (linear, mind map, Cornell) help you record and review what you hear.

textbook.com.pk Miss Hina teaches Class 9 English in a government school in Quetta. She reads her pupils a short news report about a local event and asks them what it says. The pupils can repeat the facts. She then asks them what the report assumes and what it leaves out. The pupils are silent. This topic is about moving from understanding a text to evaluating it.

Topics 2.1 and 2.2 gave you the tools: purpose, audience, context, tone, bias, assumptions, inferences, reading strategies and listening strategies. This topic asks you to apply all of them to a complete text.

textbook.com.pk When you analyse a complete text, work in four moves: Identify the surface features. What is the purpose? Who is the audience? What is the context? What is the tone? These are the features Topic 2.1 described. Identify the hidden features. What does the text assume? What can you infer? What biases or stereotypes are present? These are also from Topic 2.1, but they require deeper reading. Evaluate the strategies. Did the writer make good choices for the purpose and audience? Is the structure effective? Is the evidence adequate? This is where you move from description to judgement. Connect to your own context. Does this text work for a Pakistani classroom? Would you use it as it is, adapt it, or reject it? This is where you move from analysis to application. The figure above maps the listening process and the barriers to comprehension. Use it when you analyse spoken texts (lectures, speeches, discussions) as well as written ones.

Critical listening follows the same four moves. When you listen to a lecture, a speech or a discussion, you identify purpose, audience, context and tone; you identify assumptions, inferences and biases; you evaluate the speaker's choices; and you connect to your own context. The main difference is that spoken texts disappear as soon as they are spoken, which makes note-taking more important. Common misconception. "Critical reading means finding faults." It does not. Critical reading means understanding how a text works and evaluating whether it works well for its purpose and audience. A text can be well-written and still be biased; a text can be flawed and still be useful.

Work in groups of three. Take a short English text (a newspaper editorial, a textbook introduction, or a government pamphlet). Apply the four moves: identify surface features, identify hidden features, evaluate the strategies, connect to your Pakistani classroom context. Allow 30 minutes. Then present your analysis to another group and discuss.

Describe the four moves for analysing a complete text, in order. (Remember) A pupil says, "I understand the text but I do not know if it is good." Using this topic's account, explain what skill the pupil needs to develop. (Analyze) Explain the difference between identifying a feature of a text and evaluating it, and give one example of each. (Understand) A friend says, "Critical reading means finding faults with everything." Using this topic's account, explain what that claim overlooks. (Evaluate) A text about healthy eating assumes that all readers have access to fresh fruit and vegetables. Identify the assumption and explain what it reveals about the intended audience. (Analyze)

Analysing a complete text means identifying surface features, identifying hidden features, evaluating the writer's choices and connecting to your own context. Critical listening follows the same four moves. Critical reading means understanding how a text works, not just finding faults.

I can describe the four moves for analysing a complete text. I can apply all the skills from Topics 2.1 and 2.2 to a described text. I can distinguish between identifying a feature and evaluating it. Under the programme, schools will receive additional funding and female teachers will be given priority in recruitment. Officials say the initiative will help bridge the gender gap in literacy." The three topics follow the logic of a single reading event. Topic 2.1 asks what the writer brought to the text; Topic 2.2 asks what strategies the reader brings; Topic 2.3 asks trainees to combine both in practice. Teach them in order across the four weeks the content-spec allows.

"Reading means decoding every word." This is the most persistent one. Probe it by asking: "If you can read every word but cannot answer questions about the text, have you read it?" Trainees who equate reading with decoding will find the strategy sections counter-intuitive. "Listening is a passive skill." Probe it by asking: "If someone speaks to you in Urdu while you are thinking about something else, have you listened?" The goal is to make the case that listening requires active engagement. "Critical reading means finding faults." Probe it by asking: "Can a text be well-written and still be biased?" The goal is to shift from fault-finding to understanding how a text works.

Topic 2.1 - Analyse two texts on the same topic (25 minutes, pairs). The trap is that trainees identify purpose without explaining how they know. Push them back: "What evidence in the text tells you the purpose is X and not Y?" Topic 2.2 - Apply SQ4R to a text (30 minutes, individual). The trap is that trainees skip the "question" step and go straight to reading. Remind them: "The question is what makes you read with a purpose. Without it, you are just reading words." Topic 2.3 - Analyse a complete text (30 minutes, groups of three). This is the most cognitively demanding activity. The trap is that trainees list features without evaluating them. Push them back: "You have identified the bias. Now tell me: does it matter? Does it affect the reliability of the text?"

Each topic carries a "Try this at your practicum school" task. The unit works best when the tutor sets these up explicitly before trainees leave for practicum and debriefs them when trainees return. Topic 2.1 practicum task (compare two texts) produces a comparison. Use it to open Topic 2.2: ask trainees which reading strategies would work best for each text. Topic 2.2 practicum task (observe a reading lesson) produces an observation. Use it to make the point that many pupils are never taught reading strategies explicitly. Topic 2.3 practicum task (analyse a textbook passage) produces a full analysis. Use it to make the point that the skills from Topics 2.1 and 2.2 combine in practice.

The unit carries six figures: two concept-map figures (fig-U2-1, fig-U2-6), two flowchart figures (fig-U2-2, fig-U2-3), and two table figures (fig-U2-4, fig-U2-5). The tables are the ones trainees most often try to read as prose. Before you project any of them, ask trainees to read the column headers first and say what the table is comparing.

The 10/10/5 bank is designed to be used in two passes: the MCQs and RRQs as formative checks at the end of Topics 2.2 and 2.3, and the ERQs as a summative task at the end of the unit. ERQ 5 (the integrative item) is the one that most reliably separates trainees who have understood the unit from those who have memorised its definitions. If you use only one ERQ, use that one.

Unit 1 gave you the building blocks of English, and Unit 2 taught you to read and listen with purpose. This unit asks you to put those skills to work: to speak, present and write in ways that are clear, inclusive and suited to your audience. Communication is not just about what you say, but how you say it, to whom, and in what situation.

By the end of this unit you should be able to: Explain the principles that make communication effective (clarity, coherence, conciseness, correctness, courtesy and consideration) and apply them to spoken and written texts. Structure documents (emails, reports and letters) with a clear introduction, body and conclusion. Use inclusive language that avoids stereotypes and respects cross-cultural differences. Manage the demands of public speaking, including stage fright, voice modulation and body language. Plan and deliver a short presentation with visual aids, and handle questions confidently. Apply the conventions of informal communication, including small talk, networking and turn-taking.
Units 1 and 2. This unit assumes you can identify sentence structures, recognise purpose and audience in a text, and apply the vocabulary and grammar foundations from Unit 1.

Topic 3.1 - Principles and structure of effective communication - the principles of effective communication; structuring emails, reports and letters. Topic 3.2 - Inclusive and confident speaking - inclusive language and cross-cultural communication; managing stage fright and public speaking. Topic 3.3 - Presentations and informal communication - planning and delivering a presentation; small talk, networking and conversational skills.

The three topics move from principle to practice. Topic 3.1 sets out the principles that govern all effective communication. Topic 3.2 applies those principles to speaking, with attention to inclusivity and confidence. Topic 3.3 asks you to combine everything in presentations and informal settings. Work through them in order across the four weeks the content-spec allows.

textbook.com.pk Mr Tariq teaches Class 10 in a government school in Hyderabad, Sindh. He writes two versions of the same message to parents about a school event. The first version runs to half a page, uses long formal words, and buries the date and time in the third paragraph. The second version is three short paragraphs: the purpose, the key details (date, time, venue), and what parents need to do. Parents respond faster to the second version. This topic is about why the second version works better, and how you can produce it reliably.

Effective communication is not about using impressive words. It is about getting your message across with the least effort for your reader or listener. This topic covers six principles that make communication effective and then shows how to apply them when you structure a document.

Communication scholars describe effective communication through a set of principles often called the six Cs (Verma & Raman). They apply to both spoken and written English. Clarity means your message is easy to understand. A clear message uses simple, direct language and avoids ambiguity. "The meeting is at 3 p.m. on Friday" is clear. "The meeting is at some point towards the end of the week" is not. Coherence means your ideas are logically connected. Each sentence follows from the previous one, and the reader can see the relationship between your points. Signalling words such as "first", "however" and "therefore" help the reader follow your thinking. Conciseness means saying what you need to say without unnecessary words. Conciseness is not about writing as little as possible; it is about making every word earn its place. "Due to the fact that" can usually be replaced with "because". Correctness means your grammar, spelling, punctuation and facts are accurate. Errors in correctness distract the reader and reduce your credibility. In a formal email, a subject-verb agreement error or a wrong date can undermine the whole message. Courtesy means respecting your reader or listener. Courteous communication is polite, considers the other person's perspective, and avoids language that sounds demanding or dismissive. In Pakistani professional writing, courtesy often matters as much as clarity. Consideration means tailoring your message to your audience. A message to a colleague can be shorter and less formal than a message to a headteacher. Consideration asks: what does this person already know, and what do they need from me? The figure above maps the six principles and what each demands of you as a communicator.

textbook.com.pk Even a clear, concise message needs a structure the reader can follow. The most widely used structure has three parts: introduction, body and conclusion (Verma & Raman). The figure above maps this structure for three common document types. Introduction. State your purpose early. In an email, this is usually the first sentence: "I am writing to request ..." or "This email confirms ...". In a report, the introduction states what the report covers and why. Do not make the reader guess why you are writing. Body. Present your main points, one at a time. In a short email, the body may be a single paragraph with the key details. In a report, each section of the body covers one aspect of the topic. Use headings in longer documents so the reader can find what they need. Conclusion. Tell the reader what happens next. This may be a deadline ("Please reply by Friday"), a call to action ("I would welcome a meeting to discuss this further"), or a brief summary of the main point. End politely. The figure above compares the structure of a business email, a short report and a formal letter. Notice that all three follow the same introduction-body-conclusion pattern; the differences are in tone, length and formatting. Common misconception. "More words means better communication." It does not. A long, wordy message forces the reader to work harder to find the point. Effective communication respects the reader's time. Conciseness and clarity matter more than length.

Work in pairs. Take the following short message from a teacher to a headteacher: I am writing this email to you because I wanted to bring to your kind attention that there is a problem with the water supply in the school and it has been like this for some time now and I think something should be done about it as soon as possible because the children are facing difficulty. Rewrite the message so it is clear, concise, coherent, correct, courteous and considerate. Use the three-part structure (introduction, body, conclusion). Allow 20 minutes. Then compare your version with another pair and explain which of the six Cs you improved most.
documents.s: Activity: Rewrite for the six Cs

documents.t: Name the six principles of effective communication (the six Cs) and state what each one demands of the writer or speaker. (Remember) A pupil writes, "I wanted to inform you that the thing is that the event has been postponed." Identify which of the six Cs is weakest in this sentence and rewrite it. (Apply) Explain the difference between courtesy and consideration, and give one example of each. (Understand) A friend says, "A good email should be as long as possible so nothing is missed." Using this topic's account, explain what that claim overlooks. (Analyze) A report has no headings and no clear introduction. Identify the structural problem and explain how the three-part structure would improve it. (Analyze)

The six principles of effective communication are clarity, coherence, conciseness, correctness, courtesy and consideration. They apply to both spoken and written English. Every document, from a short email to a formal report, benefits from a three-part structure: introduction (state the purpose), body (present the points) and conclusion (say what happens next). Effective communication is not about using more words; it is about making every word earn its place.

I can name the six principles of effective communication and explain what each one demands. I can apply the six Cs to evaluate a described message and suggest improvements. I can structure an email, report or letter with a clear introduction, body and conclusion. I can explain why "more words" does not mean "better communication".

Collect one piece of written communication from the school (a notice, a letter to parents, or a report). Analyse it against the six Cs: which principles does it follow well, and which need improvement? Using the three-part structure, rewrite the weakest section. Write half a page on what you changed and why. Do not name the school or any person in your write-up.

Using this topic's account of the six Cs and the three-part structure, rewrite the email so it is clear, concise, correct and courteous. textbook.com.pk Miss Hina is asked to present her practicum report to forty teachers at a training workshop in Sukkur. Her hands shake, her voice goes quiet, and she reads every slide word for word. After the workshop a colleague says, "You knew the material; you just needed to believe you could say it." This topic is about why speaking in front of others feels difficult, and what you can do about it. It is also about making sure the language you use includes everyone in the room.

Effective communication is not only about structure and clarity. It is also about who is included by your language and how you carry yourself when you speak in front of others. This topic covers two skills that matter in every classroom and every staffroom: using inclusive language and managing the demands of public speaking.

Stereotype is a fixed, oversimplified belief about a group of people. In communication, stereotypes show up in the assumptions we make: that a headteacher must be a man, that a science teacher is unlikely to be a woman, that a pupil from a rural background cannot speak English well. Inclusive language is language that avoids these assumptions and addresses everyone on equal terms (Verma & Raman). Gender-neutral language. English has several habits that exclude or assume. Using "he" to mean "he or she", calling a group of mixed pupils "you boys", or using job titles like "headmaster" when you mean any head of school. Gender-neutral alternatives use "he or she" or rephrase in the plural ("pupils ... they"), use "headteacher" or "principal" instead of "headmaster", and use "chairperson" instead of "chairman". The figure referenced in Topic 3.1 maps these alternatives alongside the six Cs: courtesy and consideration both demand that your language does not leave people out. Avoiding stereotypes. Stereotypes are not only about gender. They are also about ethnicity, disability, region and class. A sentence like "Even the slow learners understood it" assumes that some pupils are defined by their speed. A more inclusive version says, "All pupils understood it" or "Pupils at every level understood it". The principle is the same: describe people by what they did, not by the group you have placed them in. Cross-cultural communication. Cross-cultural communication is communication between people from different cultural backgrounds, and it is the norm in Pakistani schools, where pupils and teachers may speak different first languages and come from different regions. Verma and Raman note that effective cross-cultural communicators do three things: they avoid assuming that their own way of speaking is the only correct one, they listen for meaning rather than judging accent or word choice, and they adapt their register to the listener. In a school in Karachi, a teacher might switch between Urdu and English to include a pupil who is still building confidence in English. That choice is not a failure of English; it is a success of communication.

Public speaking is speaking to a group with a purpose: to inform, persuade or explain. The guide lists it as a core skill for teachers, and the workshop vignette above shows why it matters. The figure above maps the relationship between anxiety and performance. The anxiety-confidence curve. A small amount of nervousness before speaking is normal and even useful: it sharpens your focus and gives your voice energy. As anxiety rises past a certain point, performance falls. You forget your points, your voice tightens, and you rush. The goal is not to eliminate anxiety but to keep it in the zone where it helps rather than harms you. Overcoming stage fright. Stage fright is the intense fear of speaking in front of others. Strategies that help include: preparing thoroughly (knowing your material reduces the fear of forgetting), practising out loud (rehearsal builds familiarity), starting with a deep breath (this slows your heart rate and steadies your voice), and making eye contact with one friendly face rather than scanning the whole room. Verma and Raman stress that stage fright shrinks with repeated, small exposures: speak to a pair, then a small group, then a larger one. Voice modulation. Voice modulation is the deliberate variation of your volume, pace and pitch to hold attention and convey meaning. A flat, monotone voice loses an audience even when the content is good. modulate your voice by slowing down for important points, pausing instead of filling silence with "um", and raising your volume slightly to signal a new idea. In a large hall, projecting your voice (speaking from the diaphragm, not the throat) carries further without shouting. Body language. Body language includes your posture, gestures, eye contact and facial expression. Standing with your shoulders back and your weight even signals confidence. Gesturing naturally emphasises points. Eye contact builds trust with your audience. Avoid crossing your arms, turning your back to write on the board while speaking, or gripping the podium. Your body speaks before your words do. Common misconception. "Public speaking is a natural talent, not a skill." It is not. Like classroom management or lesson planning, it is a set of techniques that improve with practice. Teachers who speak confidently in front of a staffroom have almost always practised, failed and adjusted. The anxiety-confidence curve shows that the goal is management, not magic.

This activity has two parts. Work in groups of four. Part 1 (15 minutes). Take a short text (a textbook paragraph, a school notice, or a job advertisement). Identify three phrases that assume, exclude or stereotype. Rewrite each phrase so it is inclusive. Use the figure referenced below as a guide. Part 2 (15 minutes). Each group member delivers a one-minute talk to the group on a topic they know well (a favourite lesson, a hobby, a place in Sindh). After each talk, the group gives one piece of positive feedback on voice or body language and one suggestion. The goal is practise, not perfection. textbook.com.pk The figure above maps inclusive-language guidelines with examples and alternatives. Use it as a reference for Part 1.

Explain the difference between a stereotype and an assumption, and give one example of each. (Understand) A notice says, "The chairman will address the staff at 10 a.m." Rewrite this sentence using gender-neutral language and explain the change. (Apply) A friend says, "I cannot speak in front of people because I am just not a confident person." Using the anxiety-confidence curve, explain what this claim overlooks. (Analyze) A teacher says, "Even the weakest pupils understood the lesson." Identify the stereotype in this sentence and rewrite it so it is inclusive. (Apply) Name three strategies for managing stage fright and explain how each one helps. (Remember)

Inclusive language avoids stereotypes and addresses everyone on equal terms, through gender-neutral pronouns, careful job titles and descriptions that focus on what people do rather than the group they belong to. Cross-cultural communication requires the listener to suspend judgement and adapt to the audience. Public speaking anxiety follows an anxiety-confidence curve: a little nervousness helps, too much harms, and strategies such as preparation, rehearsal, deep breathing and eye contact keep you in the helpful zone. Voice modulation and body language are skills that improve with practice, not talents you are born with.

I can identify stereotypes and assumptions in a described text and rewrite them inclusively. I can explain the anxiety-confidence curve and what it implies for managing stage fright. I can name at least three strategies for managing public speaking anxiety. I can use voice modulation and body language deliberately when I speak to a group.

Observe one school assembly or staff meeting. Note the speaker's voice (volume, pace, pauses), body language (posture, gestures, eye contact) and language (any stereotypes or inclusive choices). Write half a page on one strength and one area for improvement, with a specific suggestion drawn from this topic. Do not name the school or the speaker in your write-up.

textbook.com.pk Miss Rashida is asked to give a fifteen-minute presentation on reading strategies to a group of primary-school teachers at a training in Larkana. She has never given a formal presentation before. She wonders how to choose what to say, whether to use slides, what to do if someone asks a question she cannot answer, and how to keep to fifteen minutes. This topic walks through the whole process, from preparation to follow-up. It then covers the informal side of communication: the small talk, networking and conversational moves that make professional relationships work.

Presentations and informal communication are two sides of a teacher's professional life. A presentation is planned, structured and delivered to a group. Informal communication is unplanned, responsive and happens in hallways, staffrooms and workshops. Both require skill, and both can be learned.

Presentation skills are the abilities that let you deliver a clear, engaging talk to a group. The figure above maps the stages from preparation to follow-up (Hutchinson & Waters, 1987; Verma & Raman). 1. Define your purpose and audience. Before you decide what to say, decide why you are speaking and who is listening. Are you informing (explaining a new strategy), persuading (arguing for a change in assessment) or training (teaching a skill)? What does your audience already know? A presentation on reading strategies for experienced teachers looks different from one for first-year trainees. 2. Research and organise your content. Gather your material and organise it into the three-part structure from Topic 3.1: introduction (state your purpose and preview your points), body (two or three main points, each with an example) and conclusion (summarise and give a takeaway). Limit yourself to two or three main points. A fifteen-minute presentation cannot cover everything; choose what matters most. 3. Design visual aids. Visual aids (slides, charts, handouts) support your talk; they do not replace it. Each slide should carry one idea, use large fonts, and avoid long paragraphs. A simple diagram or a short bullet list is easier to follow than a page of text. Hutchinson and Waters note that the best visual aids are ones the audience can grasp in seconds, leaving their attention free for you. 4. Rehearse. Practise out loud, ideally in the room or a similar space. Time yourself. Rehearsal reveals points that are unclear, sections that run too long, and transitions that need work. It is the single most effective way to reduce the anxiety described in Topic 3.2. 5. Deliver. On the day, arrive early, check the equipment, and take a breath before you begin. Open with your purpose, make eye contact, and modulate your voice (Topic 3.2). Keep an eye on the clock. If you are running short, skip a minor example; do not rush the conclusion. 6. Handle Q&A. Handling Q&A means responding to audience questions confidently. Listen to the whole question before answering. If you know the answer, give it briefly. If you do not, say so honestly: "I do not have that information with me; I will find out and follow up." Audiences respect honesty more than guessing. 7. Follow up. After the presentation, share your slides or a summary if promised. Thank the organiser. Reflect on what went well and what you would change next time. This reflection is what turns one presentation into a skill you build over time. Managing time. Managing time in a presentation means planning how long each section will take and sticking to it. A useful rule of thumb: spend about ten per cent of your time on the introduction, eighty per cent on the body, and ten per cent on the conclusion and Q&A. For a fifteen-minute talk, that is roughly ninety seconds, twelve minutes and ninety seconds. Practise with a timer so you learn what twelve minutes of speaking feels like.

Informal communication is the unplanned, everyday talk that builds professional relationships: conversations in the staffroom, introductions at a workshop, a quick exchange with a parent after school. It may feel unstructured, but it follows conventions you can learn (Downes, n.d.; Verma & Raman). Small talk. Small talk is brief, light conversation about non-controversial topics: the weather, travel, a recent school event. Its purpose is not to exchange information but to build rapport. In Pakistani professional settings, small talk often includes polite enquiries about health or family before moving to business. Starting a workshop interaction with "How was your journey?" or "Is this your first visit to this city?" signals courtesy and consideration (the six Cs from Topic 3.1). Networking. Networking is building and maintaining professional relationships that support your work. Downes describes it as the skill of making a genuine connection in a short exchange: introducing yourself clearly, asking a question that shows interest, and ending with a concrete next step ("I would like to hear more about your reading programme; could we talk after the session?"). Networking is not collecting contacts; it is starting relationships. Turn-taking. Turn-taking is the convention by which speakers alternate in a conversation. Smooth turn-taking uses cues: a slight pause signals that you are finished, a raised intonation can hold your turn, and a brief "mmm" or nod signals that you are listening and the other person should continue. Interrupting or dominating a conversation breaks the norm and signals disrespect. Conversational repair. Conversational repair is what speakers do when something goes wrong: a misunderstanding, a word that does not come, or a point that was not clear. Repair strategies include rephrasing ("Let me put it differently"), asking for clarification ("Could you say more about what you mean by ...?"), and checking understanding ("So you are saying that ...?"). Repair is a sign of a skilled communicator, not a weak one. Politeness strategies. Politeness strategies are the ways speakers protect each other's dignity in interaction. They include indirectness ("Would it be possible to ...?" instead of "Do this"), hedging ("I think perhaps ..."), and showing appreciation ("I really value your point on ..."). In Pakistani professional culture, politeness often carries additional weight: a direct refusal can feel rude, so softening your language is both courteous and effective. textbook.com.pk The figure above maps conversational moves for small talk, networking and professional dialogue. Use it as a reference when you prepare for a workshop or a networking event. Common misconception. "Informal communication requires no structure." It does. Small talk has topics that are safe and topics that are not. Networking has an arc (introduce, connect, follow up). Turn-taking, repair and politeness all follow patterns. The difference from formal communication is not the absence of structure but the flexibility with which you apply it.

Work in groups of three. Part 1 (20 minutes). Choose a topic from your B.Ed course (for example, a teaching strategy, a classroom management technique, or a reading activity). Plan a five-minute presentation using the seven stages in the figure above. Prepare no more than three slides (hand-drawn on paper is fine). Decide who will present, who will time, and who will ask a question. Part 2 (15 minutes). Each group delivers their five-minute presentation to another group. The audience asks one question during Q&A and gives one piece of feedback on voice, body language or visual aids. The presenting group notes what they would change next time.

documents.t: Name the seven stages of planning and delivering a presentation, in order. (Remember) A friend says, "I will put all my notes on my slides so I do not forget anything." Using this topic's account of visual aids, explain what that approach gets wrong. (Analyze) Explain the difference between small talk and networking, and give one purpose for each. (Apply) A presenter is asked a question they cannot answer. Describe the recommended response and explain why it is better than guessing. (Apply)

A presentation follows seven stages: define purpose and audience, research and organise content, design visual aids, rehearse, deliver, handle Q&A and follow up. Time management and rehearsal are what separate a smooth presentation from a rushed one. Informal communication, far from being structureless, follows conventions: small talk builds rapport, networking builds relationships, and turn-taking, conversational repair and politeness strategies keep interactions respectful and productive. Both formal and informal communication are skills that improve with deliberate practice.

I can plan a short presentation using the seven stages from preparation to follow up. I can design visual aids that support, rather than replace, my spoken message. I can explain the difference between small talk, networking and professional dialogue. I can use turn-taking, conversational repair and politeness strategies in a described interaction.

Attend one staff meeting or workshop break. Note one example of small talk, one example of networking and one example of conversational repair or politeness. Write half a page on how each move functioned: what it achieved and what might have happened without it. Do not name the school or any person in your write-up.

Effective communication rests on six principles: clarity, coherence, conciseness, correctness, courtesy and consideration. Documents (emails, reports, letters) follow a three-part structure: introduction, body, conclusion. Inclusive language avoids stereotypes and respects cross-cultural differences. Public speaking anxiety follows an anxiety-confidence curve, and strategies such as preparation, rehearsal, voice modulation and body language help keep anxiety in the helpful zone. Presentations follow seven stages from purpose and audience definition through to follow up. Informal communication, far from being structureless, follows conventions of small talk, networking, turn-taking, conversational repair and politeness strategies.

In this unit's account, "conciseness" means: (Remember) a) using as few words as possible, even if the meaning suffers b) saying what you need to say without unnecessary words c) writing in short sentences only d) avoiding formal language A message that uses "he" to refer to a person of unknown gender fails which of the six Cs? (Understand) a) Clarity b) Conciseness c) Courtesy and consideration d) Coherence The three-part document structure recommended in this unit is: (Remember) a) title, body, references b) introduction, body, conclusion c) greeting, message, signature d) heading, paragraph, footnote A teacher replaces "chairman" with "chairperson". This is an example of: (Apply) a) voice modulation b) gender-neutral language c) conversational repair d) managing time On the anxiety-confidence curve, performance is highest when anxiety is: (Understand) a) zero b) very high c) moderate d) rising Which stage comes first when planning a presentation? (Remember) a) Design visual aids b) Rehearse c) Define purpose and audience d) Handle Q&A A presenter does not know the answer to an audience question. The recommended response is: (Apply) a) change the subject b) guess and move on c) say you do not know and offer to follow up d) repeat the question back to the audience "Turn-taking" in conversation refers to: (Remember) a) the order in which speakers alternate b) the topic of the conversation c) the volume of the speakers d) the length of the conversation A speaker who varies their volume, pace and pitch to hold attention is using: (Apply) a) conversational repair b) small talk c) voice modulation d) turn-taking A teacher says, "Even the slowest pupils finished the task." The most inclusive rewrite is: (Apply) a) "All pupils finished the task." b) "Some pupils finished the task." c) "The task was too easy." d) "The teacher finished the task."

Using this unit's account of the three-part structure, explain what is wrong and how to fix it. (Analyze) Explain the difference between courtesy and consideration, with one example of each. A colleague sends the following email to a headteacher: "I am writing to you because I wanted to bring to your kind attention that there are some problems with the classroom furniture and I think something should be done about it." Using this unit's account of the six Cs and the three-part structure, rewrite the email and explain four specific changes you made. Using this unit's account of the anxiety-confidence curve and the seven-stage planning process, write a response that (a) explains why some nervousness is normal, (b) proposes three specific strategies, and (c) justifies each strategy. Rewrite it inclusively and explain each change by reference to the six Cs. (Analyze) Evaluate the claim that "good communicators are born, not made." Use this unit's account of the six Cs, the anxiety-confidence curve and the conventions of informal communication to argue for or against the claim. (Evaluate) Integrative. You are placed in a government school where the headteacher asks you to (a) deliver a ten-minute presentation on inclusive language to the teaching staff and (b) network with visiting teachers at the tea break afterwards. Using this unit's account of presentations, informal communication and the six Cs, plan both activities. Justify each choice. (Create)

b - conciseness means saying what you need to say without unnecessary words. c - using "he" for a person of unknown gender fails courtesy and consideration. b - the three-part structure is introduction, body, conclusion. b - "chairperson" is a gender-neutral alternative to "chairman". c - on the anxiety-confidence curve, performance peaks at moderate anxiety. c - defining purpose and audience is the first stage of planning a presentation. c - the recommended response is to say you do not know and offer to follow up. a - turn-taking is the order in which speakers alternate. c - varying volume, pace and pitch is voice modulation. a - "All pupils finished the task" describes what happened without labelling any group.

The three topics move from principle to practice. Topic 3.1 sets out the six Cs and the three-part document structure that govern all effective communication. Topic 3.2 applies those principles to speaking, with attention to inclusivity and confidence. Topic 3.3 asks trainees to combine everything in presentations and informal settings. Teach them in order across the four weeks the content-spec allows.

"More words means better communication." This is the most persistent one. Probe it by asking: "If a parent receives a half-page email and a one-line email with the same information, which one will they act on faster?" Trainees who equate length with quality will find the conciseness section counter-intuitive. "Public speaking is a natural talent, not a skill." Probe it by asking: "Do you know a teacher who seemed terrified of speaking at first and now does it confidently? What changed?" The goal is to normalise the anxiety-confidence curve and to stress that practise, not talent, is what changes performance. "Informal communication requires no structure." Probe it by asking: "If you meet a senior teacher at a workshop and say nothing, has communication happened?" The goal is to make the case that small talk, networking, turn-taking and politeness all follow learnable conventions.

Topic 3.1 - Rewrite for the six Cs (20 minutes, pairs). The trap is that trainees shorten the message without improving clarity. Push them back: "You have made it shorter. Is it also clearer? Can I tell from the first sentence what you want?" Circulate and listen for explanations that link a change to a specific C. Topic 3.2 - Inclusive-language audit and mini-speak (30 minutes, groups of four). Part 1 (audit) is analytical; Part 2 (mini-speak) is the one that generates the most anxiety. Set clear ground rules: the audience gives one positive and one constructive comment, and the goal is practise, not perfection. Debrief Part 2 by asking: "What did you notice about your own nerves? Did the anxiety-confidence curve ring true?" Topic 3.3 - Plan and deliver a mini-presentation (35 minutes, groups of three). The trap is that trainees spend all their time on the slides and none on rehearsal. Remind them: "A five-minute talk needs at least one rehearsal out loud. The slides support you; they do not give the talk for you." If possible, have groups present to each other rather than to the whole class, to reduce the pressure.

Each topic carries a "Try this at your practicum school" task. The unit works best when the tutor sets these up explicitly before trainees leave for practicum and debriefs them when trainees return. Topic 3.1 practicum task (analyse a school document) produces a concrete example. Use it to open Topic 3.2: ask trainees which of the six Cs the document handled well, and link courtesy and consideration to the inclusive-language section. Topic 3.2 practicum task (observe a speaker) produces a voice-and-body-language analysis. Use it to open Topic 3.3: ask trainees how the speaker managed the room, and connect that to the delivery and Q&A stages of a presentation. Topic 3.3 practicum task (observe a meeting or break) produces examples of informal moves. Use it to make the point that communication skills are not only for formal situations; the staffroom and the workshop break are where professional relationships are built.

The unit carries six figures: one concept-map figure (fig-U3-1, the six Cs), one diagram figure (fig-U3-2, the anxiety-confidence curve), one flowchart figure (fig-U3-3, the presentation stages), and three table figures (fig-U3-5, document structure; fig-U3-6, inclusive language; fig-U3-7, conversational moves). The anxiety-confidence curve (fig-U3-2) is the one trainees most often misread as "anxiety is bad". Before you project it, ask trainees to read the three zones and say what the curve claims about moderate anxiety.

The 10/10/5 bank is designed to be used in two passes: the MCQs and RRQs as formative checks at the end of Topics 3.2 and 3.3, and the ERQs as a summative task at the end of the unit. ERQ 5 (the integrative item) is the one that most reliably separates trainees who have understood the unit from those who have memorised its definitions. If you use only one ERQ, use that one.

Units 1, 2 and 3 gave you the building blocks of English, the skills to read and listen with understanding, and the principles of effective communication. This unit asks you to put all of that to work in the kinds of writing and speaking you will do as a teacher and as a professional. Not every workplace or community communicates the same way, and a message that works in one setting can fail in another. This unit gives you the tools to write with purpose and to adapt your communication to the context.

By the end of this unit you should be able to: Identify the structure, tone and conventions of the main professional writing formats: business emails, memos, short reports and formal letters. Explain how cultural context shapes the way English is used, including high-context and low-context communication, directness, politeness and face-saving strategies. Analyse a described cross-cultural communication breakdown and identify what went wrong. Adapt the style, register and content of a message for a different cultural or professional audience.

Units 1 to 3. In particular, this unit assumes you can write clear, grammatically correct sentences (Unit 1), read a text for purpose, audience and context (Unit 2), and apply the principles of effective communication (Unit 3).

Topic 4.1 - Professional writing in practice - business emails, memos, short reports and formal letters; the writing process from draft to final version. Topic 4.2 - Intercultural communication - high-context and low-context communication; directness, politeness and face-saving strategies. Topic 4.3 - Adapting communication for your context - adapting style, register and content for diverse cultural and social contexts.

The three topics move from the page to the person to the situation. Topic 4.1 gives you the formats you will actually write. Topic 4.2 gives you the cultural knowledge to understand why the same words land differently in different settings. Topic 4.3 asks you to combine both in practice. Work through them in order.

textbook.com.pk Miss Hira has just started her first teaching job at a government high school in Hyderabad. In her first week she is asked to write four things: an email to the headteacher requesting leave, a memo to staff about a changed timetable, a short report on a school-cleanliness drive, and a formal letter to a parents' association. She knows English well, but she has never had to choose between an email, a memo, a report and a letter. This topic is about those choices.

Professional writing is not about using long words or complex sentences. It is about choosing the right format for the right purpose and audience, and then following the conventions that readers expect. Hutchinson and Waters (1987) describe English for professional purposes as a set of genres: each genre has a typical structure, a typical tone and a typical set of phrases, and learning the genre means learning to produce writing that fits the reader's expectations. textbook.com.pk The figure above maps the writing process you will use for every format this topic covers. It is rare to get a professional document right in a first draft. The process moves from planning (what is this for, who is it for) through drafting, revising (rethinking structure and content) and editing (fixing grammar, punctuation and tone) to a final version.

A business email is the most common professional writing format today. It is used to request, inform, confirm or follow up, usually within an organisation or between organisations. The structure of a business email is simple: Subject line: short and specific. "Leave request for 23 September" is better than "Request". Salutation: "Dear Mr Rashidi," or "Dear Colleagues," depending on the relationship. Opening: state your purpose in the first sentence. "I am writing to request leave on 23 September for a medical appointment." Body: give only the information the reader needs. One short paragraph is usually enough. Closing: "Thank you for your time," or "I look forward to your response," followed by a sign-off ("Yours sincerely," for someone you do not know well; "Kind regards," for someone you do). Signature: your name, role and contact details. The tone of a business email is polite and direct. It is less formal than a letter but more formal than a text message. Avoid slang, emoticons and all-capital writing. Common phrases include "I am writing to…", "Could you please…", "I would appreciate it if…", and "Please find attached…". Worked example before you write one. A poor version of Miss Hira's leave email reads: "Hi, I want leave on 23rd because I have a doctor appointment. Thanks, Hira." A better version reads: "Subject: Leave request for 23 September. Dear Mr Rashidi, I am writing to request leave on 23 September for a medical appointment. I have arranged for Mrs Kazi to cover my Classes 9 and 10 during my absence. Thank you for your consideration. Yours sincerely, Hira Ansari, Class 9 English." The second version is not longer because it tries to sound formal; it is longer because it gives the reader the information they need.

A memo (short for memorandum) is an internal document used to inform or instruct people within the same organisation. A short report is used to present findings, often to a supervisor or a small committee. Both follow a clear structure. The memo structure: To, From, Date, Subject at the top. Purpose: one sentence on why you are writing. Background: the context the reader needs. Action or information: what happened, what you found, or what you want the reader to do. Next steps or deadline, if any. The short report structure adds a little more: Title and date. Introduction: what the report is about and why it was written. Findings: what you observed or discovered, often in short paragraphs or bullet points. Conclusion and recommendation: what should happen next. Hutchinson and Waters (1987) note that both genres reward clarity over decoration: short paragraphs, plain headings, and concrete detail. A memo that says "The cleanliness drive took place on 15 September. Sixty pupils and eight teachers participated. Three areas of the school were cleaned. The committee recommends a follow-up drive in November" is more useful than a vague, wordy paragraph.

A formal letter is used for communication outside the organisation or for official communication within it: letters of complaint, request, application or recommendation. Downes (2010) describes the formal letter as the format that still carries the most weight in professional settings in South Asia, where a printed and signed letter is often expected for job applications and official requests. The formal letter structure: Your address (top right), then the date. The recipient's name and address (left). Salutation: "Dear Sir/Madam," (when you do not know the name) or "Dear Mr Khan,". Subject line (optional but common in Pakistani formal letters): "Subject: Application for the post of…" Opening paragraph: state your purpose. Body paragraphs: develop your point. Closing paragraph: state what you hope will happen next. Sign-off: "Yours faithfully," (when you wrote "Dear Sir/Madam") or "Yours sincerely," (when you used the person's name), then your signature and printed name. A job application letter (cover letter) follows the same structure. Downes (2010) advises that a strong cover letter does not repeat the CV; it picks two or three points from the CV and explains why they matter for this specific post. "I have three years of teaching experience in a government school in Sindh, including two years managing a multi-grade classroom" is more convincing than "I am hardworking and honest." Common misconception. "Professional writing means using complex vocabulary." It does not. Professional writing means matching the format, tone and level of detail to the reader and the purpose. A short, clear email is better professional writing than a long, vague letter. As Hutchinson and Waters (1987) put it, the reader is the judge of whether a piece of writing works, and the reader judges it by how easily they can find what they need.

Work in pairs. Read the following five situations and decide which format (email, memo, short report or formal letter) is most appropriate for each. For each situation, explain your choice in one sentence and draft the subject line or opening sentence. Allow 20 minutes. Then compare your choices with another pair and discuss any disagreements. You want to tell all staff that the staff meeting has moved from Monday to Wednesday. You are applying for a teaching post at a private school in Sukkur. You need to tell the headteacher that the science laboratory has no running water. The education district officer asks you to summarise enrolment trends in your school over the last three years. You want to request a meeting with the parents' association chair to discuss attendance.
documents.s: Activity: Match the format to the situation

documents.t: Name the four professional writing formats this topic covers and state the main use of each. (Remember) A colleague writes a business email with the subject line "Urgent!!! Please read now!!!!" and no clear opening sentence. Using this topic's account, explain what is wrong and how to fix it. (Analyze) Arrange these writing-process stages in the correct order and explain what happens at each: edit, draft, plan, revise, final version. (Understand) A pupil writes a job application letter that repeats every point from their CV. Using Downes (2010), explain what a stronger letter would do instead. (Apply)

Professional writing is not one skill but several. A business email is short, direct and polite, with a clear subject line and opening. A memo informs or instructs internally. A short report presents findings with a clear structure. A formal letter is the most formal of the four and is used for official and external communication. All four rely on the same writing process: plan, draft, revise, edit, final version. The reader's needs, not the writer's wish to sound impressive, decide what good professional writing looks like.

I can choose the right professional writing format for a described situation and explain why. I can draft a business email with a clear subject line, opening, body and closing. I can distinguish a memo from a short report and a formal letter. I can move a piece of writing through the writing process from plan to final version. I can identify and correct tone and structure problems in a sample professional document.

Collect one example of professional writing used in the school: a letter, a notice, a report or an email (with permission, and with names removed). Analyse it using this topic's account: which format is it, does it follow the expected structure, is the tone right for the audience, and what is one thing you would change to make it clearer? Write half a page. Do not name the school, the staff or the pupils in your write-up.
documents.s: Try this at your practicum school

documents.t: Write 350 to 400 words on the following. You are a teacher at a government school in rural Sindh. The school has no computer lab, and the headteacher has asked you to write to the district education officer requesting two computers for the school. Choose the most appropriate professional writing format, draft the document, and explain in one paragraph why you chose that format and how your draft follows its conventions. Mini-rubric Criterion What a strong response does Choice of format (Understand) Chooses the format that fits the situation and justifies the choice with reference to audience and purpose Conventions of the format (Apply) The draft follows the structure, tone and phrasing the topic describes for that format Quality of the justification (Analyze) Explains specifically how the draft's structure and tone serve the reader and the purpose, not just that it "looks formal" Register and clarity Writes for a colleague, defines any technical term used, stays within the word count

Hutchinson, T., & Waters, A. (1987). English for Specific Purposes: A Learning-Centered Approach. Cambridge University Press. Chapter 7 sets out the genre-based view of professional writing this topic draws on. Downes, C. (2010). Cambridge English for Job-hunting. Cambridge University Press. Units 2 to 4 cover formal letters and cover letters for job applications.

textbook.com.pk Mr Omar teaches in a government school in Lahore. A visiting teacher from rural Sindh, Miss Zahra, joins the staff. In a staff meeting, the headteacher asks Miss Zahra to share her teaching experience. She speaks softly, begins with a long account of her village and her training, and never directly states her main point. Some colleagues look impatient. Later, Mr Omar asks a British-trained volunteer teacher the same question. The volunteer answers in two sentences: "I focus on group work. My pupils' test scores rose last term." Same question, two very different answers. This topic explains why.

Intercultural communication is the study of how people from different cultural backgrounds communicate with one another, and how cultural assumptions shape the way messages are sent, received and interpreted. English is a global language: the English spoken in Karachi, in London, in Lahore and in New York is not used in exactly the same way. Learning to communicate across these differences is a core skill for a teacher, who works with pupils, parents and colleagues from many backgrounds.

The most influential account of cultural difference in communication comes from Hall (1976), who distinguished high-context and low-context communication. In a high-context culture, much of the meaning is carried by the context: the relationship between the speakers, the shared history, the setting, what is left unsaid. The words themselves may be indirect and understated. The listener is expected to "read between the lines". Many South Asian, East Asian and Middle Eastern communication styles are relatively high-context. Miss Zahra's long, story-like answer in the staff meeting is a high-context style: the meaning is embedded in the account, and a listener who knows the style will hear humility, respect for the group and a gradual build to the point. In a low-context culture, meaning is carried mainly by the words themselves. The speaker is expected to be explicit, direct and efficient, and the listener should not have to guess. Many Northern European, North Australian and North American communication styles are relatively low-context. The volunteer's two-sentence answer is a low-context style: the meaning is in the words, and nothing is left to inference. textbook.com.pk Neither style is better. Hall (1976) is clear that the distinction is a tendency, not a rule: every person and every conversation falls somewhere on the spectrum between the two extremes. A Pakistani doctor explaining a diagnosis to an elderly patient may use a high-context style (gentle, indirect, relationship-focused), while the same doctor writing a referral letter to a specialist uses a low-context style (precise, technical, direct). Why this matters for you. Pakistani classrooms are often high-context environments, but the English textbooks, exams and official documents pupils encounter are written in a relatively low-context style. A teacher who understands both can help pupils navigate between them.

A second dimension of intercultural variation is directness. In some cultures, saying "no" directly is honest and efficient. In other cultures, a direct "no" threatens the relationship and is avoided. Brown and Levinson (1987) describe face as the public self-image every person wants to maintain, and they distinguish two kinds: Positive face: the want to be liked, appreciated and approved of. Negative face: the want to be unimpeded, to have freedom of action without pressure. A face-saving strategy is a way of speaking that protects either your own face or the other person's face. Common face-saving strategies in English include: Hedging: softening a statement. "I wonder if you might…", "Perhaps we could…", "It might be a good idea to…". Giving reasons before a refusal: "I would love to help, but I have a prior commitment" instead of "No, I cannot". Using questions instead of commands: "Could you share the notes?" instead of "Give me the notes". Apologising: "I'm sorry, but I won't be able to attend" signals respect for the other person's invitation. These strategies are not weakness. Brown and Levinson (1987) argue that politeness is a fundamental part of human language, and every culture has its own system of it. The difference is in which face is prioritised and which strategies are considered polite. In many Pakistani settings, protecting the other person's positive face (showing warmth, respect, hospitality) is central. In some low-context Western settings, respecting negative face (not imposing) is more central. Worked example before you analyse one. Consider a parent who arrives late to a meeting with a teacher. A relatively direct (low-context) response: "You are fifteen minutes late. We started without you." A face-saving (higher-context) response: "Thank you for coming. We have just started; please join us." Both communicate the same fact (the meeting has started), but the second protects the parent's positive face and preserves the relationship. A skilled teacher chooses the response the situation and the relationship call for. Common misconception. "Cultural awareness is about memorising facts about other cultures." It is not. Facts are a starting point, but cultural awareness is the habit of noticing that your own way of communicating is not the only way, and of adjusting your style when the situation demands it. Hall (1976) warns against turning cultural tendencies into stereotypes: not every Pakistani is high-context, and not every British person is low-context. The value of the framework is that it gives you a way to notice and interpret differences, not a set of labels to apply to people.

Work in groups of three. Read the following scenario and answer the questions below. Allow 25 minutes. Then present your analysis to another group. A Pakistani teacher on an exchange programme in England emails her mentor: "I was wondering if it might be possible for you to observe my lesson next week, if it is not too much trouble. I completely understand if you are too busy. Perhaps another time would be better." The mentor reads the email as lacking confidence and assumes the teacher does not really want the observation. Using Hall's high-context / low-context framework, explain what is happening. Using Brown and Levinson's face framework, identify the face-saving strategies the teacher uses and how the mentor might interpret them. Rewrite the email so it is clearer for a low-context reader while still sounding polite.

Explain the difference between high-context and low-context communication in your own words, and give one example of each. (Remember) A colleague says, "Low-context communication is just rude." Using Hall (1976), explain what is wrong with that claim. (Understand) A pupil writes in an essay, "Tell me the answer." Rewrite the sentence using two different face-saving strategies from this topic and explain which face each one protects. (Apply) Analyse the staff-meeting scenario at the start of this topic. Identify one high-context feature of Miss Zahra's answer and one low-context feature of the volunteer's answer, and explain how each fits their likely cultural framing. (Analyze)

Intercultural communication is shaped by at least two major dimensions. Hall's (1976) high-context / low-context spectrum describes where meaning lives: in the shared context or in the words themselves. Brown and Levinson's (1987) face framework describes how politeness works: speakers use strategies to protect their own and others' positive and negative face. Neither framework ranks one style above the other; both give you tools to notice, interpret and adapt to the communication patterns you meet as a teacher.

I can explain high-context and low-context communication and recognise each in a described example. I can identify at least three face-saving strategies in a piece of spoken or written English. I can analyse a described cross-cultural communication breakdown using Hall's and Brown and Levinson's frameworks. I can rewrite a direct message in a more face-saving way without losing its meaning. I can reject the claim that one communication style is simply better than another.

Over one week, collect three examples of communication between the school and parents or the community (a letter home, a verbal request, a notice at the gate). For each, note whether the style is closer to high-context or low-context, and identify any face-saving strategies used. Write half a page on what you notice and whether the style fits the audience. Do not name the school, the staff or the families in your write-up.
